title: Self-Critical Voice Rewrite
summary: A CBT sheet where a client catches a harsh inner statement, tests it, and rewrites it in a fairer voice.
goal: Help a client notice self-critical thoughts and practice a more balanced response.
body_md: Ask the client to pick one recent harsh thought, rate how much they believe it, and look at evidence on both sides. Then draft a fairer sentence they could say to a friend. The goal is balance, not forced positivity. Re-rate the belief at the end and watch for the client dismissing the new statement as untrue.

title: Task Switch Card Game

goal: Give a client playful practice at the pause, reset, and start steps of switching between tasks.
body_md: Rules: players take turns drawing a task card, work on it for one minute, then draw a switch card with the next task. Between rounds, they say aloud the three reset steps: pause, name what is next, take the first step. Debrief on which switches felt hardest and what helped. goal: Help a client turn vague tasks into one visible, concrete next action they can start.
body_md: Choose three tasks that keep stalling and write each on a card, with the very next physical action on the back, small enough to start in two minutes. Have the client test one in session. Notice what makes a card too vague, and refine it together. Keep the cards where the task happens.

title: Boredom Willingness Practice
summary: An ACT practice in which a client notices the pull away from a dull task and practices staying with it for a short stretch.
goal: Help a client notice restlessness and choose to stay with a task that matters to them.
body_md: Pick a task that matters but is dull. The client sets a short timer, notices the urge to switch, names it, and keeps going, then writes what the urge did. The goal is willingness, not force or perfect focus. Pair it with a value so the stay has a reason, and make the stretch short enough to succeed.

goal: Help a client set up a brief weekly routine that keeps small things from piling up.
body_md: Build the checklist with the client from what actually slips: papers, calendar, messages, laundry. Keep it to five or six items they can finish in about twenty minutes, and fix a regular day and time with a cue. Expect to revise it after a week or two, and treat a missed reset as information to adjust the plan.

The parent walks the track with the child for the first days, offers a cheer at the finish, and keeps prompts brief and kind. Adjust the stops together weekly.

title: Trust Rebuilding Check-In Plan

goal: Give a couple a predictable, low-heat way to talk about recovery and rebuild trust.
body_md: Run this in session so both partners hear the agreement as it is made. The partner in recovery names what they will share and when; the other partner names what they will ask and how they will respond to hard news. Watch for the check-in turning into questioning, and help them keep it brief, scheduled and kind.

title: Saying No Practice Role-Play Cards
summary: A card game where players practice saying no to offers of substances in realistic, low-stakes scenes.
goal: Build confidence and ready phrases for turning down substance offers.
body_md: Write scenario cards together beforehand: a friend at a party, a coworker after work, a family gathering. Players draw a card, take the offerer or the refuser role, then swap. Debrief on which phrases felt natural and which felt forced. Keep it playful at first and raise realism gradually, following the client's pace.

title: Choice Point for Urges
summary: An ACT choice point map for a moment of substance use urge, sorting moves toward values and moves away.
goal: Help a client notice a hooked moment and pick the next step on purpose.
body_md: Draw the choice point with the client: the situation at the top, a fork below. Moves away from what matters are often quick relief; moves toward are usually harder in the moment. Use a recent real urge and avoid shaming the away moves, since they usually make sense. Revisit the same sheet after practice.

title: Free Time Rebuild Planner
summary: A weekly planner for filling the hours that used to belong to substance use with chosen activities.
goal: Replace empty or risky stretches of the week with planned, valued activity.
body_md: Start by listing the times of day that used to involve substance use, because those are usually the open gaps. Help the client choose activities that are realistic and personally meaningful, not just distracting. Review next session what happened, and adjust without judgment if plans fell through.

fields.label: The times of day or week that used to involve substance use
What I miss about those times, and what I do not miss
Activities I used to enjoy before substance use took over
New things I would like to try
My plan for the riskiest time block this week
Who could join me or check in
What I will do if the plan falls apart

title: Evening Self-Soothing Kit
summary: A DBT self-soothe through the five senses menu built for the hours when substance use urges tend to rise.
goal: Give a client a ready set of soothing options for urge-heavy evenings.
body_md: Work through the five senses with the client and have them name specific items they can actually get hold of on an evening: a tea, a playlist, a blanket. Stress that this does not remove urges but gives them something to do while the urge passes. Suggest keeping a physical kit and checking how it worked afterward.

fields.label: Something I can see that calms me
Something I can hear that calms me
Something I can smell that calms me
Something I can taste that calms me
Something I can touch or wear that calms me

title: Calm Down Corner Builder
summary: A child and parent build a cozy calm corner at home and decide together what goes in it.
goal: Give a child a place and a set of tools for cooling off that they chose themselves.
body_md: The parent and child gather pillows, drawing paper and sensory items and set up the corner together, with the child making the choices. The parent explains the corner is a place to get calm, not a punishment, and practices using it once when everyone is calm. If a child discloses harm at home, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: The name I gave my calm corner
Three things I picked to put in it
What my body feels like when I need to go there
What I do first when I get there
What my parent does when I am in my corner
How I know I am ready to come back out
What I want to tell my parent after I cool off

title: Cool Down Relay Game
summary: A team relay where players race to complete calming skills cards instead of racing at full speed.
goal: Make practicing cooling skills active, fun and memorable in a group.
body_md: Set up stations with calming skills such as paced breathing, a cold drink, stretching and counting. Teams take turns, and players must finish each skill slowly to score. The twist of slowing down on purpose usually lands well with teens. Debrief on which skills worked best and when in real life each would be useful.

The skill that was hardest to do slowly
What changed in my body during the relay
A moment this week when I could use that skill
What I would say to a teammate who is about to blow up
The skill I will keep in my toolkit

title: Checking the Facts on Anger
summary: A DBT check the facts sheet separating what happened from the story attached to it before acting on anger.
goal: Slow down the jump from an event to an angry reaction.
body_md: Choose a recent angry moment. Have the client describe only what a camera would have recorded, then list the interpretations and assumptions. Ask whether the emotion and its intensity fit the facts, and what action would fit. Be careful not to suggest anger is wrong; the aim is a choice about the response.

fields.label: What happened, as a camera would have recorded it
What I told myself it meant
Other possible explanations
What I was feeling and how strong it was (0 to 10)
Does the strength fit the facts, as far as I can tell?
What I wanted to do
What I could do that fits what matters to me

title: Hot Thought Rewind Sheet
summary: A CBT thought record tuned for angry thoughts, such as demands, blame and mind reading.
goal: Help a client catch and test the hot thoughts that fuel anger.
body_md: Anger thoughts often sound like 'should', 'always' and 'on purpose'. Help the client pick out the hottest thought from a recent incident, then look at the facts for and against it. Avoid arguing them out of their feelings; the goal is a more balanced thought they still believe, and a response they can choose.

fields.label: The situation that set off my anger
The hottest thought I had
Words in it like always, never, should or on purpose
Facts that fit this thought
Facts that do not fit it
A more balanced way to say it
How angry I feel now (0 to 10)

title: Anger and What I Value Compass
summary: An ACT values exercise asking what an angry moment shows about what matters and how to act on it well.
goal: Connect anger to the value underneath it and pick a response in line with it.
body_md: Many clients find anger has a value under it, such as fairness, respect or protecting someone. Help them name that value and then compare what anger-driven actions cost against what value-driven actions would look like. Avoid framing anger as a problem to remove; the point is room to choose a response.

fields.label: A recent time I was angry
What I was trying to protect or stand up for
The value underneath it, in a word or two
What I did when angry, and what it cost
What acting on that value could look like instead

title: Mental Ritual Spotter
summary: A worksheet to help a client notice hidden mental rituals such as checking, reviewing and counting in the head.
goal: Help a client see the covert rituals that keep an intrusive thought cycle going.
body_md: Many people only count visible actions as rituals and miss what happens in the head. Go through the list with curiosity and not criticism, and let the client sort what actually feels like a ritual from ordinary thinking. This is a noticing tool for you to work from, and it does not replace your own judgment.

fields.label: An intrusive thought that shows up for me
What I do in my head right after it (review, repeat, check, argue)
How long I spend doing that
What I hope it will do for me
What happens to the thought afterward

One I would like to watch for this week

title: Doubt Dial Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment where a client rates a feared outcome, tries a doubtful situation, and compares.
goal: Let a client test what happens when they tolerate doubt without checking.
body_md: Choose a small, specific feared prediction with the client and agree on the exact experiment. They rate their belief in the prediction before and after, noting what they did instead of the ritual. Keep it modest at first, and discuss results without pushing certainty, since the lesson is about living with some doubt.

fields.label: The doubt or fear I am testing
What I predict will happen
How much I believe that (0 to 100)
What I will do, and what I will not do (my usual ritual)
What actually happened

What I learned about doubt

title: Values Before Rituals Direction Sheet
summary: An ACT compass comparing time given to rituals with time given to what matters in the client's life.
goal: Help a client see what rituals take from valued living and where to redirect.
body_md: Ask the client to name their values in several areas of life, then estimate how much time rituals take from each. This can bring up grief or frustration, so give it room. Choose one small, values-based action to do in the place of a ritual-heavy stretch, and keep the language kind and free of blame.

fields.label: Three things that matter most to me
How rituals take time from each of those
A time of day when rituals take the most
What I would like to do with that time
What I fear might happen if I did it
A small values step I will try this week
What I will say to myself if the urge to ritualize gets loud

title: Supportive Not Reassuring Phrase Card
summary: Partners write supportive replies that care for the person without answering the doubt.
goal: Help a partner support their loved one without feeding the reassurance cycle.
body_md: Work with the partner who is asked for reassurance to draft warm replies that recognize feelings and leave the question unanswered, and with the partner who experiences OCD to say what kind of reply would help them. Role-play a few. Expect the supporting partner to feel guilty about holding back, and name that.

fields.label: Partner with intrusive thoughts: how I ask for reassurance
Partner with intrusive thoughts: what kind of reply helps me later
Supporting partner: how it feels to be asked

title: Thought Bubble Pass Game
summary: A group game where intrusive-style thoughts on cards are passed along and acknowledged without reacting.
goal: Practice letting a thought be there without acting on it, through play.
body_md: Write neutral, silly or mildly uncomfortable thoughts on cards, avoiding anything graphic or truly distressing. Players pass the card clockwise and say, 'I notice a thought that...' then hand it on. Choose content to fit the group so no one is flooded. Debrief on how it felt to notice without arguing or fixing.

fields.label: A thought that was easy to pass along
A thought that felt harder to pass
What I noticed in my body
What I wanted to do when the thought arrived
What it was like to just say 'I notice a thought'

title: Calm Breathing Pinwheel Craft
summary: A child makes a pinwheel and uses it to practice slow, steady breaths with a parent.
goal: Give a child a hands-on way to practice slowing their breathing.
body_md: The child decorates and builds a paper pinwheel, then practices blowing it gently and slowly with the parent. Explain that fast breathing is part of how a body gets ready to be brave, and practice when calm so it is familiar. The parent models along with the child. Follow reporting duties if a child discloses harm.

fields.label: The colors I picked for my pinwheel
What my body feels like when it gets really scared
What happens to my pinwheel when I breathe fast
What happens when I breathe slow
Who I practiced with

How I felt after the slow breaths

title: Sensation Surprise Card Game
summary: A card game where players safely bring on harmless body sensations and rate how strong and how safe they feel.
goal: Practice noticing body sensations without alarm in a playful, structured way.
body_md: Cards name safe activities such as spinning slowly, breathing through a straw or jogging in place. Players take a turn, rate the sensation, and say what they noticed. Choose cards to fit the client's health, and use your judgment on pacing. Debrief on what the sensations felt like and what thoughts came with them.

fields.label: The card I drew
The sensations I noticed
How strong they felt (0 to 10)
The thought that came with them
What happened to the sensation after a minute
A sensation that surprised me

title: Safety Behavior Inventory
summary: A worksheet listing the things a client does to feel safe around panic, and what each costs them.
goal: Help a client see which safety habits keep life small.
body_md: Safety behaviors such as carrying water, sitting near exits or checking a pulse can feel necessary. List them without criticism and note what each one gives and costs. Choose with the client which to test dropping first, if any, and in what order. This is a conversation starter for your own clinical judgment.

fields.label: Things I carry or keep close in case of panic
Places or seats I choose to feel safe
Things I check in my body
What each one gives me
What each one costs me
Which one I might try without first, and when
What I expect to happen if I do

title: Panic Prediction Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment where a client records what they predict during panic and what actually happened.
goal: Compare feared predictions about panic sensations with real outcomes.
body_md: Ask the client to write their prediction when a panic wave begins, such as 'I will faint', and then note what happened. Review a few entries together and look for patterns, such as predictions that did not come true. Keep it curious and not argumentative, and leave medical questions to the client's doctor.

fields.label: Where I was when the panic wave started
What I felt in my body
What I predicted would happen
How sure I was (0 to 100)
What actually happened
How long the strongest part lasted
What I notice across my entries

title: Making Room for Alarm Practice
summary: An ACT practice for letting panic sensations be present while moving toward something that matters.
goal: Practice making room for alarm sensations while doing what the client values.
body_md: Guide the client to notice panic sensations, name them, breathe around them and keep doing a small valued activity anyway. This is not about getting rid of panic. Use a mild sensation first and pace to the client's comfort. Ask afterward what it was like to carry the feeling along instead of fighting it.

fields.label: A valued activity I want to do even with panic around
Sensations I notice when alarm shows up
How I usually fight or escape them
What it would look like to make room for them
What I noticed when I tried
What I did anyway
What I will practice this week

title: Tantrum Storm Shelter Plan
summary: A parent and child build a cozy calm-down shelter and decide together how it gets used.
goal: Give a child and parent a shared, practiced place and script for big feelings.
body_md: Have the parent and child build a small shelter from pillows and a blanket, then decorate it with calming items the child picks. The point is rehearsal while everyone is calm, so the shelter is a place the child chooses rather than a punishment. Coach the parent to stay nearby and quiet. If a child discloses anything worrying, remember your reporting duties.

fields.label: The name my child gave our shelter
Three things we put inside it to help us feel calm
The words the parent will say when a storm starts
What my child wants the parent to do while they are inside
How we will know the storm has passed
When we will practice using the shelter this week

title: Sibling Squabble Referee Game
summary: A turn-taking card game where siblings and parents practice fair solutions to common arguments.
goal: Let siblings rehearse fair, calm solutions to everyday arguments through play.
body_md: Write common squabbles on cards, such as who sits where or whose turn it is. Players draw a card, act as the referee, and propose a fair fix, with the parent playing too and sometimes giving a deliberately unfair answer for the children to catch. In the debrief, ask which fixes felt fair to everyone. Keep it silly so the children stay open to it.

fields.label: A squabble card we drew
The fix I suggested as referee
Whether everyone felt it was fair, and why
A squabble from home we could try a fix on
A fair fix we want to remember
What the parent will do next time a squabble starts

title: Good Enough Parent Thought Swap
summary: A thought-swap sheet that pairs harsh parenting thoughts with balanced, realistic alternatives.
goal: Help a parent notice perfectionistic parenting thoughts and test more balanced ones.
body_md: Walk the parent through one recent moment when they judged themselves harshly, then separate the situation, the thought and the feeling. Ask them to write a balanced alternative they could believe at least partly. Parents often write what sounds nice but feels untrue, so ask for a rating of belief before and after. Use it alongside your own formulation of the parent's patterns.

fields.label: The parenting moment I judged myself about
The thought that showed up, in my own words
How strongly I believed it, from 0 to 100
What I would say to a friend in the same spot
A more balanced thought I can partly believe
How strongly I believe the balanced thought now

title: Hooked Parent Defusion Cards
summary: Cards that help a parent notice sticky parenting thoughts and hold them lightly while acting on values.
goal: Help a parent unhook from rigid parenting stories and act on what matters to them.
body_md: Ask the parent to name the stories that grab them in hard moments, such as I am failing or my child should not act like this, and write each as a card beginning with I am having the thought that. Practice saying the cards aloud, then choose one small values-based parenting action to take with the thought still present. Keep the tone playful rather than corrective.

fields.label: A sticky story I tell myself as a parent
The same story starting with I am having the thought that
What the thought pushes me to do
What I want my parenting to stand for
One small action I can take with the thought still there
How I will notice when I get hooked this week

title: Parenting Partners Weekly Check-In
summary: Two parents each name what is working, what feels heavy and what support they want from each other.
goal: Give two parents a short, structured way to align and support each other each week.
body_md: Each partner fills in their own part, then they take turns reading aloud while the other listens without fixing. Partner A speaks first one week and Partner B the next. Watch for the check-in turning into a list of complaints; steer back to one request each. Use it as a bridge between sessions and adapt it to the family's rhythm.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciated about how we parented this week
Partner B: something I appreciated about how we parented this week
Partner A: what felt heaviest for me this week
Partner B: what felt heaviest for me this week
Partner A: one specific thing I would like help with
Partner B: one specific thing I would like help with

title: Nighttime Worry Parking Lot
summary: A bedside worksheet where a new parent parks worries on paper and plans a time to revisit them.
goal: Help a new parent set down nighttime worries and sort which ones need action.
body_md: Introduce this as a bedside page for the worries that show up during night feeds or waking. The parent jots each worry, then marks whether it has an action for tomorrow or is a what-if to let sit. Review together how it went; many parents find the act of writing helps but need permission to keep it brief. Adapt it to what the parent is carrying.

fields.label: The worry on my mind right now
Whether it needs an action tomorrow or is a what-if
If it needs action, the one small step I can take
A kind thing I can tell myself while I wait
When I will look at this page in daylight
Who I could share the heavy worries with

title: Wise Mind Moments for New Parents
summary: A brief wise-mind practice a new parent can use between feeds, matching feeling and reasoning.
goal: Give a new parent a quick way to find a steady, balanced response in tiring moments.
body_md: Teach wise mind as the place where feeling and reasoning overlap, and practice it with one recent moment of overwhelm. Ask the parent to name what the emotional mind said, what the reasonable mind said, and what wise mind suggests. Keep the practice short enough to fit between feeds. Check in on how realistic each step is given how little sleep they are getting.

fields.label: A recent moment I felt overwhelmed
What my emotional mind said
What my reasonable mind said
What my wise mind says, in one sentence
One breath or pause I can use before the next feed
A cue in my day that will remind me to try this

title: Visitor Boundaries Script Sheet
summary: A script sheet for setting kind limits on visitors, advice and help in the weeks after a baby arrives.
goal: Help a new parent plan clear, warm limits around visitors and unsolicited advice.
body_md: Many new parents feel guilty saying no to well-meaning family. Use the sheet to name which visits and offers they want, and to draft short sentences they can say or text. Rehearse one or two aloud in session so the words are familiar. The goal is the parent's comfort, not a rulebook; let them decide what to include and revisit it as needs change.

fields.label: Who I want to see in the next few weeks
How long and how often feels manageable
What kind of help I would like most
A kind sentence I can use to say not yet
A sentence I can use when advice is not welcome
Who will help me say these things if I freeze

title: Newborn Care Card Swap
summary: Partners sort caregiving and household tasks onto cards and trade them to find a sustainable shape.
goal: Help two new parents see all the care work and renegotiate who does what.
body_md: Write every task, from night feeds to laundry to remembering appointments, on cards, including the invisible mental load. Each partner sorts the cards into who does it now, then they swap two or three cards and name the part they will each take. Name both partners' parts in the summary. Expect tiredness to color the conversation, so keep each turn short and kind.

fields.label: Partner A: tasks I carry right now
Partner B: tasks I carry right now
Partner A: one card I would like to swap and why
Partner B: one card I would like to swap and why
Partner A: what I will take on this week
Partner B: what I will take on this week

title: Mixed Feelings Welcome Practice
summary: An acceptance practice for making room for joy, grief and ambivalence all at once after a baby arrives.
goal: Help a new parent allow mixed feelings about parenthood without judging them.
body_md: Invite the parent to name all the feelings present, including ones they think they should not have, and to notice they can coexist with caring for the baby. Use a simple willingness exercise where each feeling gets a place at the table. Be alert for shame; normalize that mixed feelings are common and leave it to your judgment whether other support is needed.

fields.label: A feeling about this new chapter that is easy to say
A feeling I find harder to admit
Where I notice each feeling in my body
What I tell myself about having these feelings
What I would say to a friend who felt the same
One small thing I care about that I can do with the feelings still here

title: Inner Critic Comic Strip
summary: A child draws their inner critic and a kind helper as comic characters and scripts their conversation.
goal: Help a child separate from a harsh inner voice and practice a kinder reply.
body_md: Have the child draw a three-panel comic: the critic says something mean, the helper responds, and the child decides what to do. Let them design the characters however they like. Invite the parent to listen to the finished comic and to say one thing they appreciate about the child. If a child shares anything worrying, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What my inner critic looks like
What the critic says that bothers me
What my kind helper looks like
What the helper says back
What I decide to do next
Who I could show this comic to

title: Compliment Receiving Rehearsal
summary: A skills sheet for taking in praise with a simple thank-you and noticing the urge to deflect.
goal: Help a client practice accepting a compliment without discounting it.
body_md: Role-play receiving a compliment, noticing the urge to deflect or return one at once. Link it to describing and mindful attention: notice the words, the feeling and the urge, then say thank you and stop. Many clients find this much harder than it sounds, so start with small compliments and let them choose how much to practice outside session.

fields.label: A compliment I got recently
What I said back
What I felt in my body when I heard it
The urge I noticed to push the compliment away
A simple thank-you I can say instead
A time this week I will practice just saying thanks

title: Good Enough Standards Experiment
summary: A behavioral experiment that tests what happens when a task is done to a good enough standard.
goal: Help a client test whether lowering a perfectionist standard changes the feared outcome.
body_md: Pick one small task where the client holds a very high standard, and plan to do it at a good enough level on purpose. Record the prediction, the outcome and what they noticed. Keep the experiment small and agree on it beforehand. Review the result with curiosity and let your clinical judgment guide whether to raise the stakes in the next one.

fields.label: The task and the standard I usually hold
What I think will happen if I do it at good enough
How strongly I believe that, from 0 to 100
What I actually did
What actually happened
What I take from this about my standards

title: Worth Is Not Earned Phrase Cards
summary: Defusion phrase cards for the stories that tie a person's worth to performance or approval.
goal: Help a client hold worth-based stories lightly and choose actions by values.
body_md: Ask the client to write the I am only worth it if stories on cards, then practice noticing them as thoughts with silly voices or by saying them slowly. Follow with one action chosen from a value, taken with the story still present. Keep the aim on flexibility rather than winning an argument with the thought.

How it sounds when I say it slowly

title: Strengths Charades Game
summary: A group guessing game where players act out strengths seen in themselves and each other.
goal: Give a group a playful way to name strengths and receive recognition from others.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a strength card, such as patient or brave, and acting out a time they used it while others guess. After each round, someone else adds a time they saw that strength in the player. Debrief by asking what it was like to hear it. Expect some embarrassment and let players pass on a turn.

title: Small Talk Role-Play Deck
summary: A card deck for practicing openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits in low-stakes role-plays.
goal: Let a client practice small talk skills in a playful, low-pressure setting.
body_md: Make cards with settings like a line at a coffee shop and prompts like ask a follow-up question. Players draw, role-play for a minute and the clinician or group gives one thing that went well. Keep the stakes low and let clients choose their level of challenge. In the debrief ask what they predicted versus what happened.

title: Blushing and Shaking Acceptance Practice
summary: A practice for letting visible anxiety signs be present while staying engaged in a conversation.
goal: Help a client stay engaged in social moments with visible anxiety present.
body_md: Explore which visible signs, such as blushing, shaky hands or a trembling voice, the client fears others will notice. Practice letting them be there during a short role-play while the client keeps attention on the other person and their value of connection. Avoid framing the goal as getting rid of the signs. Let your judgment shape the pace.

title: Social Event Teammate Plan
summary: A pre-event plan where partners agree on signals, breaks and how to debrief afterward.
goal: Help partners support each other through a social event without pressure or rescue.
body_md: The partner who feels social anxiety names what would help, and the other partner names what they can offer without taking over. Agree on a break signal, how long to stay and a kind debrief afterward. Name both partners' parts. Watch for the supporting partner answering for the other; coach them to let the person take their own turns.

title: Hello Challenge Passport
summary: A child collects stamps for small, brave social steps like saying hello, with the parent coaching from the side.
goal: Help a child take small social steps with a parent cheering from nearby.
body_md: Draw a passport together and list small social steps, such as waving at a neighbor or asking a friend a question. The child chooses one at a time and the parent coaches and cheers without doing it for them. Praise the trying, not the outcome. If a child discloses anything worrying, remember your reporting duties.

title: Social Avoidance Cost Ledger
summary: A ledger that lists what avoiding social situations has protected and what it has cost.
goal: Help a client weigh the short-term relief of avoidance against its costs.
body_md: Ask the client to list situations they avoid, what the avoidance gives them in the moment and what it has taken from their life. Work toward the client's own words about what they want back. Avoid arguing them out of the relief; the relief is real. Use the ledger to choose a first small step together.

title: Anniversary Ritual Designer
summary: A planning sheet for shaping a meaningful ritual around a birthday, anniversary or holiday after a loss.
goal: Help a client plan a chosen way to mark a hard date with support.
body_md: Use this before a hard date, such as a birthday, to help the client choose how they would like to mark it, who to invite and what to do if feelings rise. Rituals can be tiny. Respect that some clients want nothing, which is also a plan. Check how realistic their plan is and what support they have.

What I would like the day to hold
Who I would like to share it with
Something that reminds me of the person or what I lost

title: Grief Five Senses Comfort Kit
summary: A self-soothing kit built from the five senses to use during waves of grief.
goal: Help a client build a ready kit of comforts for waves of grief.
body_md: Walk through each sense and have the client pick one thing that soothes without avoiding the grief, such as a scent, a song or a soft blanket. Prepare the kit in session so it is ready before a wave arrives. Reinforce that comfort is not forgetting. If a client mentions thoughts of harming themselves, move to your own safety steps in session.

title: Grief Feelings Color Map
summary: A child colors a body outline with the feelings of grief and talks with a parent about each color.
goal: Help a child name grief feelings through color and share them with a parent.
body_md: Give the child a body outline and invite them to choose colors for feelings like sad, mad, worried and missing. They fill in where they feel each one. The parent listens and says what they notice without fixing. Let the child lead and stop whenever they wish. If a child discloses anything worrying, remember your reporting duties.

The color I picked for each one

title: Pain of Love Valuing Practice
summary: A practice linking the pain of loss to what the client valued in the person and in their life.
goal: Help a client hold grief and love together and choose values-based actions.
body_md: Invite the client to notice that grief is bound up with what mattered, then name the values the relationship embodied. Choose one small action that carries a value forward, such as kindness or humor, while the pain is present. Avoid rushing toward meaning. Let them lead and use your own judgment about pace.

fields.label: What I miss most about the person or what I lost
The value that relationship stood for
How the pain and love feel together
One small way I could carry that value forward

title: Hard Day Prediction Check
summary: A sheet comparing predictions about a hard day with what actually happened afterward.
goal: Help a client test predictions about difficult dates and notice what helped.
body_md: Before a hard day, the client writes predictions about how it will go and what they will not be able to handle. Afterward, they record what happened and what helped. Reflect on the gap with curiosity, but never push the idea that grief should feel better. Use it as a conversation starter in your own formulation.

fields.label: The hard day I am preparing for
What I predict will happen
How strongly I believe it, from 0 to 100
What helped me get through it
What actually happened
What I want to remember for next time

title: Weekly State of Us Check-In
summary: A short weekly sheet for one partner to name what felt close, what felt strained, and one small request.
goal: Give a client a steady, low-stakes way to bring relationship concerns into session.
body_md: Have the client fill this in once a week, ideally on the same day, and bring it to session. It gives you a quick read on what the client notices about the relationship over time without turning each week into a verdict. Watch for requests that are really complaints, and help the client reshape them into something specific and doable.

fields.label: One moment this week when I felt close to my partner
One moment when I felt distant or tense
What I was feeling and needing in that tense moment
One small, doable request I could make this week
One thing I will do on my side

title: GIVE Skill Rehearsal Card
summary: A rehearsal card for the GIVE interpersonal skill, gentle, interested, validate, easy manner, in one real conversation.
goal: Help a client practice keeping the relationship intact while raising a hard topic.
body_md: Walk the client through each letter of GIVE, then rehearse the opening minute of a real upcoming conversation in session. Clients often hear gentle as giving in, so name the difference. Have them pick just one or two letters to focus on first, and debrief on how the practice felt in the body as well as in the words.

fields.label: The conversation I want to have, and with whom
How I can be gentle in my first sentence
A question showing I am interested in their side
Something I can validate, even if I disagree
What an easy manner would look like for me

title: Partner Assumption Check-Out Sheet
summary: A thought sheet that separates what a partner did from the story the client adds about why.
goal: Help a client notice assumptions about a partner's motives and test them gently.
body_md: Use this after a recent moment of hurt or irritation. The client separates the observable event from the meaning they assigned, then rates how sure they feel and lists other possible explanations. The aim is a wider view, not proof that the partner meant well. Pair it with a plan to ask the partner directly when it feels safe to do so.

fields.label: What my partner said or did, as a camera would record it
The story I told myself about why
How sure I felt in that story, 0 to 100
Two other things that could explain it

How I feel now after looking at it again

title: Soft Startup Rewrite Game
summary: A turn-taking card game where players rewrite harsh complaint openers into gentler, specific ones.
goal: Build fluency with raising a concern without blame, using humor and low stakes.
body_md: Write a dozen harsh openers on cards, such as 'You never help.' Players take turns drawing one and rewriting it as a soft startup: feeling, situation, small request. The group votes on the version that would land best. In the debrief, ask what made the rewrites easier or harder, and let couples try one on a real topic only if they choose to.

fields.label: The harshest opener I drew
My rewrite using a feeling, a situation, and a request
What the group liked about the best rewrite
What was hard about softening it

title: Family Meeting Speaking Token Craft
summary: A child decorates a talking stick that is passed around at family meetings so everyone gets a turn.
goal: Give a family a concrete cue for taking turns when something needs to be discussed.
body_md: The child decorates a stick or cardboard tube with drawings of what makes a good listener. The parent then explains the rule: only the holder talks, and everyone else listens. Try it in session with a light topic like a weekend plan. Parents should model waiting and reflecting back what they heard, and keep early meetings short and positive.

fields.label: Draw or write what a good listener does
Draw or write what I want my family to know about me
One thing that would make our home feel calmer
One fun topic for our first family meeting

title: Pacing Dial for Hard Days
summary: A simple dial sheet that helps a client decide how much to take on today and what to set aside.
goal: Support a client in pacing daily demands and choosing gentler options on hard days.
body_md: Introduce this as a way to keep the client in charge of pace, not a measure of progress. The client rates how today feels, then sorts tasks into do now, do small, and wait. It stays entirely in the present and asks for no account of the past. Revisit it in session so the client can notice that slowing down is a choice and a skill.

fields.label: On a scale of 1 to 10, how hard does today feel

What I can do in a smaller way today

title: Window of Tolerance Check-In
summary: A card for noticing whether the body is too revved up, too shut down, or steady, and picking a skill to match.
goal: Help a client name their present-moment state and choose a stabilizing skill.
body_md: Teach the idea of a steady zone with revved-up and shut-down edges, then have the client mark where they are right now. Match each state with a skill the client already knows, such as cold water for revved-up or movement for shut-down. Keep it about the present moment only. Practice in session so the client trusts the card before they use it alone.

title: Anchors in the Present Practice
summary: A dropping-anchor style exercise to feel feet, notice surroundings, and return to the room when old reminders surface.
goal: Give a client a short way to come back to the present without having to push anything away.
body_md: Guide the client through noticing their feet, their breath, and five things in the room, while letting any thoughts or feelings be present without engaging them. Offer eyes open as the default and let the client choose. Do not ask what the reminder was about. Practice in session first, then suggest short rehearsals at calm moments rather than only during hard ones.

Five things I could see in the room
What I could hear or feel against my skin

title: Circle of Trusted Adults Hand Map
summary: A child traces a hand and writes or draws a trusted adult on each finger to name who they could tell.
goal: Help a child identify trusted adults and practice who they would go to if something felt wrong.
body_md: The child traces a hand and draws or names five trusted adults, one per finger, with the parent. Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact, focused on who helps rather than on what might happen. If a child discloses anything, stay calm, believe them, and follow your reporting duties. Parents should keep the map somewhere visible at home.

fields.label: Draw or write one grown-up I trust at home
Draw or write one grown-up I trust at school
Draw or write one grown-up in my family I could tell

What my parent will do when I tell them something

title: Safe Person Evidence Sheet
summary: A sheet for gathering present-day evidence about who in a client's life has shown steady, respectful behavior.
goal: Help a client notice trustworthy behavior in the present when trust feels hard to calibrate.
body_md: Many clients find trust swings between all and nothing. This sheet lists specific behaviors a person has shown over time, such as keeping their word or respecting a no, rather than rating the person as safe or unsafe. Go at the client's pace and never ask for details of past events. Use it to plan small, chosen steps of closeness.

fields.label: A person in my life I am considering
Times they respected a boundary or a no
Times they kept their word
Times I felt uneasy, and what exactly happened
What this suggests about how much to share for now
A small step I choose, and a step I will not take yet

title: Coping Skill Weather Forecast
summary: A planning sheet that matches coping skills to emotional weather: sunny, cloudy, stormy, and foggy days.
goal: Help a client build a ready plan so the right skill is easy to find in each emotional state.
body_md: Have the client name what each kind of day feels like in the body and mind, then choose one or two skills for each. The metaphor makes the plan easy to remember and lets the client notice that different days call for different tools. Revisit it after a week and swap out anything that did not help, without treating that as failure.

What a cloudy day feels like, and a skill that helps
What a stormy day feels like, and a skill for it
What a foggy day feels like, and a skill for it

title: Thought-Then-Skill Pairing Card
summary: A card pairing common unhelpful thoughts with a coping skill and a more balanced thought to say next.
goal: Link a client's recurring thoughts to a skill so the response is ready before the moment hits.
body_md: Ask the client for two or three thoughts that come up often when stress rises, then pair each with a skill and a balanced alternative. Rehearse reading the card aloud in session. The card works best when the balanced thought sounds like the client, not like a slogan, so edit the wording together until it fits.

title: Dropping Anchor for Hard Moments
summary: A brief exercise to feel the body, notice surroundings, and choose a next step while a hard feeling is present.
goal: Teach a client a portable way to steady themselves without needing the feeling to go away.
body_md: Lead the client through acknowledging what is showing up, connecting with the body by pushing feet down or stretching, and then noticing the room and engaging in the next task. Stress that the feeling does not have to leave. Have the client practice it twice in session and rate how it felt, then pick two moments in the week to try it.

fields.label: What I notice showing up inside right now
What I did to connect with my body
What I noticed around me in the room
What I want to do next that matters to me

title: TIPP Skill Practice Card
summary: A practice card for the TIPP skills, temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation.
goal: Let a client try each fast-acting body skill in a calm moment so they can reach for it under stress.
body_md: Go through each TIPP skill and let the client try a short version in session when they are calm, with their own consent and comfort. Check for any health concerns with the client before cold water or exercise. Clients often skip practice until they are in distress, so schedule rehearsals and have them note which skill suited them best.

fields.label: How I felt in my body before trying a skill
What happened when I tried cold water or a cold pack
What happened when I tried brisk movement
What happened when I tried slow breathing with a longer exhale
What happened when I tried tensing then relaxing my muscles

title: Coping Skill Mime Game
summary: Players act out a coping skill without words while others guess it, then share when they have used it.
goal: Make coping skills memorable and normal to talk about through movement and laughter.
body_md: Write skills on cards, such as walking, calling a friend, or slow breathing. Players take turns acting one out silently while others guess. After each correct guess, the actor says when a similar skill helped them. Debrief by asking which skills people want to try and keep the mood light so nobody feels singled out.

fields.label: The skill I acted out

A skill someone else acted that I want to try

title: Avoidance Cost Ledger for Feared Situations
summary: A two-column ledger listing what avoiding a feared situation protects and what it costs the client's life.
goal: Help a client see the full picture of what avoidance has given and taken before choosing steps.
body_md: Have the client list what avoidance gives them, usually relief, and what it takes, such as trips, jobs, or time with people. The ledger does not argue against the fear. It opens a conversation about what the client wants. Let them lead, and use it to decide if and when to build a gradual set of steps together.

title: Fear-Driven Safety Habits Inventory
summary: A list for noticing small things a client does to feel safe around a feared situation and what each one teaches the mind.
goal: Help a client spot subtle protective habits that keep the fear feeling necessary.
body_md: Safety behaviors can be quiet, like carrying a phone, sitting by the exit, or staying with someone. Ask the client to list theirs and mark which are used most. Explore, without pressure, how each one may keep the fear going. Choose one small behavior to drop in a planned step, and check how the client feels before and after.

fields.label: A situation that makes me afraid

title: Willing Steps Toward a Feared Situation
summary: A sheet connecting a client's values to one small step toward a feared situation, with room for fear to come along.
goal: Help a client choose a step they are willing to take with fear present, tied to what matters.
body_md: Begin with what the client would want to be doing if fear took up less space, then name one small step toward it. Make willingness the focus: the fear may come along. Let the client set the size of the step and a plan for what they will do with thoughts and sensations that show up. Review without judgment, whether or not the step happened.

title: Fear Thermometer Craft
summary: A child builds a paper thermometer to show how big a fear feels and move the marker as they practice.
goal: Give a child a visual, playful way to show how big a fear feels and to notice it changing.
body_md: The child builds a paper thermometer with a sliding marker and colors each level, with the parent helping. During practice, the child moves the marker to show how big the fear feels, and the parent responds with calm curiosity rather than reassurance. Choose small steps together, and praise brave tries over results. If a child discloses unsafe situations, follow your reporting duties.

Where the marker is when I think about it

title: Brave Dice Challenge
summary: A dice game where each roll picks a small brave step from a list the client built, with a debrief after each turn.
goal: Make gradual practice feel playful and shared, with the client in charge of the steps.
body_md: Before play, the client and clinician list six steps from easier to harder and number them. On each turn the client rolls and tries the matching step, or passes or swaps it for one of equal size. Take turns doing a small brave act of your own to share the risk. In the debrief, ask what they noticed, not whether it was done right.

title: Compliment Redirect Sheet
summary: A sheet for noticing appearance compliments and comments and practicing replies that move toward other topics.
goal: Help a client respond to appearance talk in ways that fit their values.
body_md: Ask the client to collect times they hear appearance comments or give them. Together, brainstorm replies that are simple and true, such as a thank-you and a topic change. Rehearse a few aloud in session. This does not tell the client what to feel about their body. It gives them more choices about the conversations they join.

title: Comparison Trigger Thought Record
summary: A thought record for moments of comparing appearance to others, separating the trigger, the thought, and a wider view.
goal: Help a client slow down automatic comparisons and respond with a more balanced thought.
body_md: Use this when the client reports comparing themselves to others online or in person. They record the trigger, the automatic thought, and the emotion, then look at what the comparison leaves out and what they would say to a friend. Do not push for positive thoughts. A believable, balanced one is enough, and the client can rate how much they believe it.

title: Values Beyond Appearance Collage
summary: A collage activity connecting the person a client wants to be to actions that do not depend on how they look.
goal: Help a client put their energy toward values-led living, with appearance as one part of the picture.
body_md: The client gathers images, words, or drawings for what they care about, such as friendship, creativity, or curiosity, and then links each to an action for the coming week. Thoughts about appearance may show up while they work, so practice noticing them and returning to the task. Keep the focus on direction, not on convincing the client to like how they look.

title: Opposite Action for Hiding Practice
summary: A card walking a client through using opposite action when shame about appearance urges hiding or avoiding.
goal: Help a client act against urges to hide or avoid, in small and chosen ways.
body_md: Teach opposite action: when an emotion urges a behavior that does not fit the situation, act in the opposite way. Have the client list hiding urges, such as skipping events or covering up, and pick one small opposite step. First check whether the emotion fits the facts. Debrief after the step on what shifted, with no pressure for a particular result.

title: Superpower Body Badge Craft
summary: A child designs a badge showing something their body can do that they are proud of, such as running, hugging, or laughing.
goal: Help a child build pride in what their body does, in a way that is playful and not about looks.
body_md: The child decorates a badge naming a body superpower, such as strong legs for jumping or hands for building. The parent joins by making a badge too, using a function and not appearance. Talk about how bodies are different and that each one is useful in its own ways. Parents should model this kind of talk at home and avoid commenting on looks, their own included.
